newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Peasants put off decision on coalition.
newsitem.headline: Polish Peasants put off decision on coalition.

text.p: The Polish Peasant party (PSL) on Friday denounced the abrupt sacking of one of its cabinet ministers but put off any decision on whether to quit the ruling coalition dominated by an ex-communist grouping.
"We do not want to take decisions in a hasty or surprising manner," Peasant leader Waldemar Pawlak told reporters after a meeting of the party's angered chiefs in Warsaw.

He said Wednesday's dismissal of Foreign Trade Minister Jacek Buchacz by Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz of the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), was arrogant behaviour that breached the coalition pact.
But the possibility that the Peasants might pull out and thereby provoke early elections appeared to diminish.

Pawlak demanded the full reasons for the dismissal of Buchacz, saying explanations published by the prime minister were inadequate, and said the Peasants might seek a meeting of both parliamentary parties to review how the coalition worked.
The SLD said it wanted the coalition to stay in place until parliamentary elections, scheduled late next year.

"We aim at solving our country's problems quietly, within the current coalition, until the end of this parliament's term," SLD leader Jozef Oleksy told a news conference. He added the elections were likely to be held in October, 1997.

The coalition has survived many rows, two sweeping cabinet reshuffles and growing policy differences between the two parties since the 1993 elections, when they beat parties rooted in the pre-1989 struggle against communist rule.

The firing of Buchacz, over what the government said was a blurring of private and public interests in granting of export guarantees, coincided with the parties rowing over cabinet posts during a reorganisation of ministries due this year.
Peasant leaders said before the meeting on Friday that they would demand an apology and other concessions including changes to the draft budget for 1997.

Some said their party wanted to head key new economic ministries, being created under a gradual reform of central government due to start in October, so as to balance the authority of the SLD prime minister which is set to increase.

Pawlak said he would renew his party's calls for a complete, one-off cabinet reshuffle to share out the new posts, although the SLD has insisted that new ministers be appointed individually, as each new portfolio comes into being.
The SLD's response and its further behaviour would determine the fate of the coalition, Pawlak said ominously.
Despite the tough talk, however, analysts said the Peasants did not have a strong hand because an end to the coalition could serve their partner's political interests.

The SLD has been leading in opinion polls, but its support has been slipping and a late August survey by the OBOP agency showed it running level at 21 percent with an opposition election alliance formed around the Solidarity union.

Early polls would allow it to campaign before the slide goes any further, while an SLD minority government, backed by the party's former leader, President Aleksander Kwasniewski, would be able to craft a 1997 budget designed to win voters.
For this reason some PSL strategists, whose party now has only about 10 percent support, see the sacking of Buchacz as an SLD provocation and caution against quitting the coalition now.
